title: Flapjacks
subtitle: Chewy oat slices with golden syrup and butter
excerpt: Thick, chewy bars made from oats, butter, golden syrup, and sugar, baked until just set with a fudgy centre and crisp edges. The easiest traybake and one of the most popular.

recipe.sourceNotes: The British flapjack is a baked oat bar made from rolled oats, butter, sugar, and golden syrup. It is distinct from the North American flapjack (which means pancake in the United States). The word flapjack has been used in English since at least the seventeenth century to mean various kinds of flat baked goods; its application to the oat traybake is a twentieth-century British usage. The flapjack became established as a tea-time bake, children's lunch box staple, and energy snack. The key to the right texture is the ratio of oats to syrup and the baking time: too long and the flapjack becomes hard and brittle; too short and it will not set. The flapjack should feel just set and slightly underdone in the centre when it comes out of the oven, as it continues to firm up significantly as it cools. It should be cut while still warm but left in the tin to cool completely.

recipeTools.notes: A 20 x 20 cm baking tin, greased and lined.

content.text: Take the flapjack out of the oven when it looks underdone: it should be golden at the edges and slightly unset in the centre. It will firm up completely as it cools. If baked until it looks done in the oven, it will be rock-hard when cold. Cut into bars while still warm, using a sharp knife, but leave in the tin until completely cold before lifting out. Store in an airtight tin for up to a week.

Heat the oven to 170 C / fan 150 C / gas 3. Grease and line a 20 x 20 cm tin. Melt the butter, golden syrup, and brown sugar together in a large saucepan over low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Remove from the heat.
Tip the oats and salt into the pan and stir to coat thoroughly. Tip into the prepared tin and press firmly and evenly with the back of a spoon. The mixture should be compact and level.
Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until golden at the edges and just set in the centre. Cut into 16 bars while still warm. Leave in the tin to cool completely before lifting out.
